title: A/L ICT: Structures and Systems
description: A/L work on the ideas behind the code: stacks and queues, recursion, sorting cost, error handling, normalisation and how a request actually travels a network.

learnBlocks.content: Two structures, two orders. A stack serves the newest item first, a queue the oldest.

lines.text: Two structures, two orders. A stack serves the newest item first, a queue the oldest.
The back button is a stack. A printer job list is a queue.
Last in first out for the stack, first in first out for the queue. That single choice changes the behaviour entirely.

evaluateBlocks.question: Match each situation to the structure behind it.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Going back returns to the most recent page, while a printer serves jobs in arrival order.

evaluateBlocks.question: Items 1, 2 and 3 are pushed onto a stack. Which comes off first?
evaluateBlocks.explanation: A stack is last in, first out, so the most recently pushed item leaves first.

evaluateBlocks.question: A queue receives A, then B, then C. In what order are they served?
evaluateBlocks.explanation: A queue is first in, first out, so they leave in the order they arrived.

learnBlocks.content: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.

lines.text: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.
Only if there is a base case. That is the line that returns without calling again.
It runs until the call stack overflows. The base case is not optional.

metadata.title: Factorial by recursion
metadata.instruction: Run it, then remove the base case and see what Python says. Put it back afterwards.
metadata.hint: Each call waits for the one below it before it can return.

learnBlocks.content: Every recursive function needs two parts: a **base case** that stops, and a **recursive case** that moves closer to it. Losing either one is the whole class of recursion bugs.

evaluateBlocks.question: What happens to a recursive function with no base case?
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Nothing stops the calls, so the stack fills and Python raises a RecursionError.

targets.label: It recurses until the call stack overflows

evaluateBlocks.question: Match each line of factorial to its role.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: The if line stops the recursion; the return line moves one step closer to it.

evaluateBlocks.question: Trace factorial(3). Put the returns in the order they actually happen.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: The deepest call returns first, and each caller multiplies on the way back up.

learnBlocks.content: Bubble sort is easy to write and slow to run. That is why it is taught and never shipped.

lines.text: Bubble sort is easy to write and slow to run. That is why it is taught and never shipped.
Its work grows with the square of the data. Ten times the data means a hundred times the work.
It does. Merge sort grows far more gently, which is why real libraries use that family.

metadata.title: Bubble sort, counting swaps
metadata.instruction: Run it, then start from an already sorted list and compare the swap count.
metadata.hint: The inner loop shrinks each pass, because the largest value has already bubbled to the end.

learnBlocks.content:
**Bubble sort**: simple, quadratic, fine for a handful of items.

**Merge sort**: splits, sorts each half, then merges. Its cost grows as n log n, which is the difference between usable and unusable on real data.

evaluateBlocks.question: A bubble sort handles 100 items. Roughly how much work for 1000 items?
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Quadratic growth squares the factor: ten times the data is a hundred times the work.

evaluateBlocks.question: Put one pass of bubble sort in order.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Each pass walks the list once and pushes the largest remaining value to the end.

steps.label: Swap them if they are the wrong way round
End the pass with the largest value at the end

evaluateBlocks.question: Match each algorithm to how its cost grows.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Those three growth shapes cover almost everything on the A/L paper.

items.label: With the square of the data

learnBlocks.content: A program that crashes on bad input is not finished, it is a draft.

lines.text: A program that crashes on bad input is not finished, it is a draft.
No. Catch what you can actually handle, and let the rest surface.
Because a swallowed error becomes a silent wrong answer, and those are far worse than a crash.

metadata.title: Handle one specific failure
metadata.instruction: Run it, then change except ZeroDivisionError to a bare except and think about what else it now hides.
metadata.hint: A bare except catches typing errors in your own code too, which is exactly the problem.

learnBlocks.content: Catch the **specific** exception you expect. A bare `except` also swallows your own typos, and then the bug hides instead of announcing itself.

evaluateBlocks.question: Why is a bare except considered poor practice?
evaluateBlocks.explanation: It catches every exception, so a NameError in your own code is silently swallowed with the expected one.

targets.label: It hides unrelated bugs, including your own typos
It only breaks the style guide

evaluateBlocks.question: Switch on the failures worth catching in a marks program.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Catch what a user or the environment can do to you. Your own typo should crash loudly so you fix it.

switches.label: A user typing letters where a number is expected
A misspelled variable name in your own code

evaluateBlocks.question: Put a robust input routine in order.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Validation happens before use, and a clear message beats a traceback for anyone who is not the developer.

steps.label: Check it is the right shape
Handle the failure with a message
Proceed with a value you trust

learnBlocks.content: Normalisation sounds abstract until you meet a table that repeats a phone number in forty rows.

lines.text: Normalisation sounds abstract until you meet a table that repeats a phone number in forty rows.
Then it is urgent. First normal form removes repeating groups, second removes partial dependencies.
Third removes fields that depend on another non-key field rather than on the key itself.

learnBlocks.content:
Unnormalised:
Student(index_no, name, subject1, subject2, subject3)

First normal form:
Student(index_no, name)
Enrolment(index_no, subject)
The test for third normal form: does every non-key field depend on **the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key**?

evaluateBlocks.question: Put the normal forms in the order they are applied.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Each form assumes the previous one has already been reached.

steps.label: Remove partial dependencies on part of a composite key

evaluateBlocks.question: A table stores class_teacher, which depends on class rather than on the student key. Which form fixes it?
evaluateBlocks.explanation: A non-key field depending on another non-key field is exactly what third normal form removes.

evaluateBlocks.question: Switch on what normalisation is actually buying you.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Normalisation buys consistency. It often adds joins, so some queries get slower, which is the trade it makes.

switches.label: Each fact lives in one place
Updates cannot leave rows contradicting each other

waves.title: 3. What Happens When You Open a Page

learnBlocks.content: Typing an address does more work than most people ever see.

lines.text: Typing an address does more work than most people ever see.
The name is turned into an address by DNS, then a connection is opened to that address.
Then a request goes out, a response comes back, and the browser builds the page from it.

learnBlocks.content: **DNS** turns a name into an address. **TCP** opens a reliable connection. **HTTP** carries the request and the response. **HTTPS** is the same thing inside encryption.
When a page fails, ask which step broke. A DNS failure, a refused connection and a 500 response are three different problems with three different fixes.

evaluateBlocks.question: Put the steps of loading a web page in order.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Name to address, address to connection, connection to request, request to page.

steps.label: Look up the name to get an address
Open a connection to that address
Build the page from the response

evaluateBlocks.question: Match each failure to the step that broke.
evaluateBlocks.explanation: Each symptom points at exactly one stage, which is what makes this worth memorising.

evaluateBlocks.question: What does HTTPS add over HTTP?
evaluateBlocks.explanation: HTTPS is HTTP inside an encrypted connection, so the content cannot be read or altered in transit.

targets.label: Encryption of the request and response
